source: Sathyanathan, Vasisht, Pruthi (2026) Evaluating Reasoning Models for Queries with Presuppositions
finding: Reasoning models are only slightly better than non-reasoning versions at challenging false claims placed in a user's query. They become more decisive, so more of their wrong answers confirm the false claim.
numbers: About 13K claims, 5 presupposition levels (neutral to writing demand). Reasoning gives +2 to +11 points factual accuracy. Models still fail to challenge 26-42% of false presuppositions overall and 37-70% at level 4. Models: GPT-OSS 20B, Qwen3 8B/32B, GPT-5 Mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash/Pro, run Dec 2025. Judge F1 0.93 on 400 human-labelled items. Of 240 failures read by hand: 57% voiced doubt in the trace, 82% of those made a small factual slip that then spread, 43% selectively presented evidence, 12% invented evidence.
quote: reasoning models outputs are also more decisive, which is reflected as a reduction in fewer equivocal responses
limits: Synthetic queries written by an LLM. One response per query for GPT-5 Mini and Gemini. Tests plain reasoning, no premise-check scaffold. Claims are factual (health, science, Wikipedia), not Moses-style word swaps.
agent_relevance: Thinking longer does not by itself catch false premises, and a user-stated premise pushes models toward agreeing. A scaffold needs an explicit step that asks 'is the premise true?' before a case is built. Do not rely on the thinking budget.

source: Zhu et al. (2025, v3 Oct 2025) Cancer-Myth: Evaluating LLMs on patient questions with false presuppositions
finding: On 585 expert-checked patient questions with a hidden false premise, no frontier model corrected the premise more than 43% of the time. Good medical answers did not mean premise correction.
numbers: Presupposition correction rate: GPT-5 42.1%, Gemini-2.5-Pro 41.4%, Claude-4-Sonnet 40.0%, Gemini-1.5-Pro 27.2%, GPT-4o 5.8%. Multi-agent MDAgents with GPT-4o did no better than plain GPT-4o.
limits: Adversarial set built to fool models, so rates are lower than on natural queries. Medical domain, GPT-4o judge.
agent_relevance: Current 2025 frontier models still miss most embedded false premises in context-rich questions. A premise-check step is worth testing, but see d03 for the cost of over-flagging.

source: Zhu et al. (2025) Cancer-Myth, mitigation experiment (precaution prompts via GEPA)
finding: The only direct test of a 'be careful about false premises' prompt on frontier models in this series. It raises premise detection a lot, but also makes the model flag premises that are fine, and it lowers scores on other tasks.
numbers: Abstract: precaution prompts with GEPA optimisation reach up to 80% on Cancer-Myth, but misidentify presuppositions in 41% of the 150 no-false-premise questions and cut other medical benchmarks by about 10% relative. Table 1 (row labels garbled in text extraction, so read with care): one model 41 to 88 on Cancer-Myth while the clean set falls 96 to 68; another 12 to 68 with clean set 88 to 59; a monitor variant 2 to 81 with clean set 90 to 35.
quote: adding precautionary prompts with GEPA optimization, can raise accuracy on Cancer-Myth to 80%
limits: Prompts were optimised on a mix of 7 medical benchmarks, so this is not an equal-token test and not a general scaffold. Table rows assigned to models by position, not certain.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 1: a premise check helps detection, yet false alarms are a real cost. Any premise-check step must be scored on clean questions too, and should fire only on a stated reason.

source: Kirichenko, Ibrahim, Chaudhuri, Bell (2025) AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
finding: Across 20 datasets (false premise, underspecified, unknown, subjective, outdated), reasoning fine-tuning lowers abstention even where accuracy rises. A system prompt that lists when to abstain helps.
numbers: 20 frontier LLMs. Reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 Distill Llama 70B, s1.1 32B) lose 24% abstention on average against their instruct bases. Setup: 4k thinking tokens plus 4k answer tokens, with a budget sweep 512-4096. Models often invent the missing context. A purpose-written system prompt raises abstention for standard and reasoning models without a significant fall in abstention precision.
quote: reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention (by 24% on average), even for math and science domains
limits: Abstention is judged by a Llama 3.1 8B judge. Only two reasoning models were compared with their bases. No Moses-type word swaps. The prompt was not run at equal total tokens.
agent_relevance: More thinking can mean more invention of missing premises. Supports an explicit 'what is not given?' check and permission to say 'cannot tell', not a longer free chain of thought.

source: Shafiei, Saffari, Moosavi (2025) MultiHoax: a dataset of multi-hop false-premise questions
finding: When a false premise is buried in the second hop of a question, six models rarely reject it. Claude (the question generator) is best but still below half.
numbers: 700 questions, 7 countries, 10 categories. Structured JSON-format accuracy: Claude 0.46, GPT 0.20, Gemini 0.18, Qwen 0.22. Average over six models by category ranged from 0.19 (entertainment) to 0.31 (science and technology). A response counts only if the model picks 'I do not know' and then correctly justifies it as a false premise.
limits: Models are from early 2025 and include small open ones. The answer set has an explicit 'I do not know' option, which may simplify the task. Claude wrote the questions, so it may have a generator advantage.
agent_relevance: Hidden multi-step premises are the hard case; a one-line premise warning is unlikely to be enough. Supports a step that checks each hop's assumption.

source: Sieker, Lachenmaier, Zarriess (2025) LLMs struggle to reject false presuppositions when misinformation stakes are high
finding: Models accommodate false presupposed content in German political questions. Rejection depends on trigger type, embedding and how likely the scenario is.
numbers: Rejection of false presuppositions: GPT-4o 84.08%, Llama-3-8B 50.05%, Mistral 2.44% (Mistral accommodated 91.51%). Scenario probability had a significant effect on rejection (chi-square(2)=7.35, p<.05). Embedding context mattered for Llama.
limits: Three models, one domain (German party politics), hand annotation. GPT-4o is not a 2026 frontier model.
agent_relevance: The best model of that study still accepted about 16% of false presuppositions. More plausible false premises are accepted more often, as with people and close Moses impostors.

source: Su and Cardie (2026) Knowing but Not Showing: LLMs recognise ambiguity but rarely ask clarifying questions
finding: Models can say a question is ambiguous when asked, but when they just answer they almost never ask. Retrieved context makes asking even rarer.
numbers: 10 models (GPT-4.1, 4o, 4, 3.5-Turbo, 4o-mini, 4.1-mini; Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Haiku; Qwen2.5 7B/14B). GPT-4 scores about 90% on unambiguous questions but 15-27% on ambiguous. Clarifying-question rate is at most about 5% (Claude highest, ambiguous questions, no context). Retrieved context lifts ambiguous-question QA accuracy from 46% to 55% and lowers asking.
quote: models can recognize that a query is ambiguous when explicitly asked to judge it
limits: Models are 2023-2025 era, QA setting not agentic. Ambiguity labels come from the dataset, not from users.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: default behaviour is to assume, not to ask. A scaffold that asks must force a recognition-to-action step, because recognition alone does not surface.

source: Pu et al. (2026, v2 Mar 2026) LHAW: Controllable Underspecification for Long-Horizon Tasks
finding: In long agent tasks with details removed, an ask-user tool recovers a lot of lost score, but models differ in how often and how well they ask.
numbers: MCP-Atlas, TheAgentCompany, SWE-Bench Pro. On MCP-Atlas, Opus-4.5 recovers to 78% pass@3 with ask_user from 47% without (100% on the full task). MCP-Atlas Ask% and Gain/Q (checkpoint gain per question): Opus 4.5 73%, 0.11; GPT-5.2 63%, 0.05; Sonnet 4.5 0.13. Gemini-3-Pro asks in only 18% of TheAgentCompany trials yet gets the best Gain/Q of any model-benchmark pair there (0.24). Of trials with questions, GPT-5.2 over-clarified in 38% and Gemini models under-clarified in 31%; under-clarification rises to 48% when the task fails.
quote: GPT-5.2 over-clarifies while Gemini models under-clarify
limits: Cost of asking is performance per question, not tokens; simulated users. Token cost not equalised against always-assume.
agent_relevance: Best current data for gap 4. Asking helps, but gain per question varies about 3x across models. A rule that asks only when the missing item is outcome-critical fits the data.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) CLAMBER: benchmark of identifying and clarifying ambiguous information needs
finding: Older models cannot reliably judge whether a query is ambiguous; chain-of-thought and few-shot prompts add little and raise overconfidence.
numbers: 12K items over an ambiguity taxonomy. Reported: only marginal gains in identifying ambiguity from CoT and few-shot prompting.
quote: These techniques may result in overconfidence in LLMs and yield only marginal enhancements in identifying ambiguity
limits: 2024 models only. Abstract and introduction read; tables not examined.
agent_relevance: Do not lean on free CoT to decide when to ask.

source: Arai and Ren (2026) DRInQ: evaluating conversational implicature with controlled context variation
finding: Models still pick readings that humans judge too strong for the context. Explicit step-by-step scaffolds raise small models a lot and large models little.
numbers: Best model GPT-4o 76% on the human-verified hard subset against a human average of 89%; most models cluster near 60% (400 items, mean of 3 runs). Reasoning-oriented GPT and DeepSeek variants beat chat variants. Scaffold prompts on the full set: gpt-5-nano 41% to 73%, gpt-5-mini 71% to 81%, gpt-4o 82% ceiling. The 'pragmatic reasoning' prompt (surface question, then contextual evidence, then inferred intent) gave the largest gain. Large models: little or no effect. Differences of 1-2 points are within noise.
quote: models frequently select interpretations that humans judge as overly strong or insufficiently supported
limits: Question utterances only, multiple choice. Authors used explanation prompts instead of CoT on purpose. GPT-4o helped write the data, which may favour it.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: context-heavy gaps are not closed in 2026 models; the error is over-commitment to a possible reading. A 'surface, evidence, speaker intent' routine is a candidate S1 step, mostly useful for small models.

source: Qiu, Zhang, Tenenbaum, Kim, Levy (2025) On the Same Wavelength? Pragmatic reasoning in LMs across broad concepts
finding: On a clue-guessing game, big models reach near-human comprehension without CoT or RSA. CoT helps comprehension and production a little. RSA helps production but adds nothing on top of CoT.
numbers: 708 human participants. The best model of each family correlates above 0.9 with human mean judgments. Small models (e.g. Qwen3 8B) are poor near scale extremes. Direct-RSA improves on Direct, but CoT-RSA does not improve on CoT.
limits: Graded numeric concept task, not implicature as in Ruis. Open models up to Qwen3 32B plus API models.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 counter-point: for graded, context-light pragmatics the gap is closed in strong models and CoT is optional.

source: Dentella, Guenther, Murphy, Marcus, Leivada (2024) Testing AI on language comprehension tasks reveals insensitivity to underlying meaning
finding: Seven models answered each comprehension question three times. Answers often changed between runs, and models did worse than 400 humans.
numbers: 26,680 data points. Mean accuracy: ChatGPT-4 0.83, Llama2 0.66, Falcon 0.66, Mixtral at chance, Bard below chance. Item stability (all three answers identical): lowest model 0.66. Answers more stable in the one-word than the open-length setting (chi-square(1)=5.16, p=.023); accuracy also higher in one-word (chi-square(1)=82.6).
limits: Authors are known sceptics. Models from 2023-early 2024. No self-consistency vote was tried, so voting at equal tokens remains untested.
agent_relevance: One sample is a noisy judge of comprehension for older models. Voting is plausible but untested here.

source: Amouyal, Meltzer-Asscher, Berant (2025) Comparing human and LM sentence processing difficulty, thinking models
finding: Thinking helps once a model is big enough. It helps evenly on non-garden-path structures but often reduces performance on garden-path ones, with GPT-5 the main exception.
numbers: o3 reaches 74.5% without thinking and GPT-5 88.9% with thinking (all structures). Garden-path structures are relatively harder than others for OpenAI models. Absolute thinking gain 0.17 on GP against 0.35 elsewhere. Weak DeepSeek and Qwen models are hurt by thinking.
limits: No test of a paraphrase or role-listing step. Human data used timed presentation.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open: plain thinking is the wrong tool for reanalysis. A role-listing scaffold is untested.

source: Speckmann and Unkelbach (2021) Moses, money, and multiple-choice: the Moses illusion in a multiple-choice format with high incentives
finding: Replicates the Moses illusion in multiple-choice format. The 52.3% figure often quoted is Erickson and Mattson's rate (as described here); this paper's own rates are 49% and 52.6%. Money has only a weak effect.
numbers: Exp 1: 49% Moses responses (M=9.73 of 20 vs chance 6.67, d=0.71, t(97)=7.10). Exp 2: 52.6% (M=10.52, t(199)=11.75, d=0.83; fixed vs shuffled options p=.259). Reder and Kusbit literal condition for comparison: 33% (Exp 1), 35% (Exp 2-3), 32% (Exp 4). Incentives: linear trend significant in Exp 3 (t(312)=2.44) but weak, not significant in Exp 4 (t(295)=1.26; main effect F(2,295)=1.07). Erickson and Mattson as described here: 52.3% over four questions (Study 1), 26.5% in the true/false focus version (Study 2).
limits: Erickson and Mattson (1981) and Ferreira (2003) primary text were not available this session; their numbers here are Speckmann's description.
agent_relevance: Correction for gap 5: about 52% is E and M and Speckmann replicates at 49-53%. Reder and Kusbit's 32-35% is from an instructed-literal condition. Even with money, people miss about half.

source: Pu et al. (2026) LHAW, agent strategy and user-cost analysis
finding: Planning-style agents ask more and do slightly better on hard underspecified tasks. The value of a question depends on who answers it, which sets how much asking is worth.
numbers: With the user reintroduced on outcome-critical tasks, Reflexion and Plan-and-Execute scored best (17.9% and 18.4%) with about 4 points better checkpoint score than ReAct and CodeAct. Persona test: asking a supervisor gave Ckpt 64.9% at Gain/Q 0.09; asking an executive gave Ckpt 56% at Gain/Q 0.13.
limits: One model (GPT-5.2) and one benchmark (TheAgentCompany) for the strategy comparison. Simulated users.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: asking pays more when it is costly to ask and the question is chosen well. Planning before acting surfaces missing items, which fits a scaffold with an explicit gaps-check state.

source: Sathyanathan et al. (2026) presupposition strength effect in reasoning models
finding: The stronger the user's wording, the more reasoning models agree with a false claim. Neutral phrasing like 'can you verify whether' gets the best behaviour.
numbers: Five levels: neutral, mild, unequivocal, writing request, writing demand. False-claim agreement grows more slowly with reasoning, but at level 4 models still back 37-70% of false claims.
limits: Level wording is LLM-written. Per-model tables (Tables 4-10) not individually read.
agent_relevance: A scaffold can neutralise the question first: restate the user's request as a neutral check before answering. This is untested, but the design follows from the measured effect of wording.
